verdict.reasoning: Patient reports “hurting when I… pee” and “pain kind of lowered down in my tummy,” which the clinician later summarizes as “burning pain on passing urine, a bit of crampy tummy pain lower down.”

The clinician summarizes: “the last three days you’ve been having a bit of burning pain on passing urine,” and earlier the patient notes it has been “going on for a few days.” A 3‑day history is a reasonable approximation.

Patient says she gets “some like, pain kind of lowered down in my tummy,” describes it as “sort of cramping,” and when asked about radiation to back or flank she answers “No, not really. No,” indicating non‑radiating crampy lower abdominal pain.
In response to blood in urine: “There was a little bit of blood earlier today.”
Patient states: “It does kind of… doesn’t smell very. Smells a bit weird, I guess,” indicating altered urine smell.
When asked about fevers: “Any fevers or temperatures?” Patient replies: “No fever.”
When asked about going to the toilet more often: “Have you found yourself going to the toilet more often than normal?” Patient replies: “I don’t think so… I haven’t noticed it, no.”
The clinician summarizes: “no other fevers or back pain, if I understand correctly,” and the patient does not contradict this, supporting denial of back pain.

Patient describes dysuria, lower abdominal pain, slight hematuria, and odor change; there is no explicit statement that she denies all other urinary symptoms beyond frequency and color. Claim that she denies other urinary symptoms is not documented.
Regarding medical history: “in the past I’ve had some… some ibs, but other than that… no serious medical problems.”
Patient reports: “I did a little bit ago or a couple days ago try some over the counter bicarbonate to try and help with the pain, but it wasn’t really helping.”
When asked about regular medications: “Do you take any regular medications?” Patient: “No,” indicating no regular meds.
Allergy history: “Yeah, I’m allergic to clindamycin.”
When asked what happens: “I get some like a swelling, basically,” indicating clindamycin causes swelling.
Sexual history: “are you currently sexually active?” Patient: “Yeah, I am with a regular partner.” Contraception: “Yeah, we use condoms.”
Social history: “I live in a… flat near my college with a couple like friends of mine… I’m a student… I’m studying biology.”
Regarding alcohol: “I do drink, like on the weekends, socially.”
Regarding smoking: “I don’t. I don’t smoke.”

The encounter is history only; the clinician says, “at this stage, I would proceed to examination,” but no exam findings are documented. Stating no notable objective findings were documented based on history is consistent with transcript.
Clinician: “Probably do have what we call a simple UTI or a urinary tract infection.”
Clinician explicitly: “Probably do have what we call a simple UTI… Symptoms are framed as consistent with a simple urinary tract infection of the bladder.”
Plan: “I’ll give you a course of antibiotics today, something called either nitroferentoin or trimethoprine. And it’s normally a three day course, so one tablet twice a day for three days.”
Advice: “I also advise you to drink plenty of fluids. Let’s try and flush that… infection out your body.”
Clinician: “You can try cranberry juice. That can sometimes help with your symptoms.”

When asked about sex: “if you can try and avoid it, I think that’d be sensible… if you can avoid it while your symptoms clear up, that’ll probably be the best,” which is advice to avoid sexual activity until symptoms resolve.

Follow-up: “if you’re still not better by the end of this week, I want you to give me a call or come back and see me… do give me a call if you have any concerns,” indicating follow up if no improvement or concerns/worsening.

Warnings: “things to look out for would be… high temperatures, back pain, just generally feeling more unwell… then we do worry whether your infection may be spreading up.” Fever and back pain are specified concerning symptoms.
